one_liner: PostgreSQL JIT provider with sljit, AsmJit and MIR backends; compiles typical queries in 0.05-1 ms where llvmjit takes 20-60 ms.
what_it_does: pg_jitter is a PostgreSQL 14-18 extension that implements the JitProviderCallbacks interface, so it replaces llvmjit by setting jit_provider ('pg_jitter_sljit', 'pg_jitter_asmjit', 'pg_jitter_mir', or the 'pg_jitter' meta-provider that switches backends per session through SET pg_jitter.backend). It walks ExprState->steps[], emits native code for hot opcodes (arithmetic, comparisons, variable access, tuple deforming, aggregate transitions, jumps) and calls PostgreSQL's ExecEval* functions for the rest. No SQL or application change is needed beyond lowering jit_above_cost.
how_it_is_fast: Compile time: it generates machine code directly through lightweight code generators (sljit, AsmJit, MIR) instead of building LLVM IR, inlining PostgreSQL bitcode and running LLVM's optimizer, which is where llvmjit's tens of milliseconds go. Execution: hot functions are emitted inline (Tier 0) or called directly without fmgr/FunctionCallInfo (Tier 1), tuple deforming is specialised per TupleDesc with an L1I-size-derived switch from unrolled to loop form, and several rewrites change the algorithm rather than the code: monotonic CASE chains and integer IN lists become precompiled binary searches (CRC32C hash probing above 4096 elements), and LIKE/ILIKE/regex go to PCRE2 JIT and StringZilla SIMD search.
when_to_use: Analytical or reporting queries in the 10 ms to seconds range where llvmjit's 20-60 ms compile cost (seconds on 100-1000-column tables) wipes out its gain, and you want JIT on with jit_above_cost around 200-2000.

Queries dominated by ILIKE, regex, long CASE ladders or large integer IN lists: the PG18 page shows 2.5-4.9x over the interpreter on ILIKE/regex and 2-7x on CASE_eq/CASE_lt_50-100 because these are algorithmic rewrites, not just compiled code.
Expression-heavy scans and joins on integer columns over wide-ish rows (10-300 columns), where the page shows roughly 1.1-1.3x over the interpreter.

Teams that cannot or do not want to ship an LLVM build with PostgreSQL; the backends are small C/C++ libraries, and the sljit backend also builds and passes regression tests on Linux ppc64le and s390x.
when_not_to_use: OLTP point lookups and sub-5 ms queries: the README itself warns of up to about 1 ms of extra execution after JIT, and the PG18 page shows a fixed cost of about 2-2.4 ms even when nothing was compiled (COUNT_star 39.4 vs 37.0 ms, UNION_ALL_agg 97.5 vs 95.5 ms with no compile time recorded; derived from page data, probably per-connection provider loading).
Workloads dominated by numeric, jsonb, array or plain text equality: the backends still call PostgreSQL's C functions and measured 0.90-1.03x of the interpreter there.

Production systems that cannot tolerate wrong results: open issue #84 (2026-08-17, no reply) reports `SELECT (SELECT 0) > 0.1` returning true under pg_jitter_sljit on PG 17.9 while llvmjit is correct, and the README calls the code beta quality.

When you want vendor support or a fast bug turnaround: one maintainer, no commits since 2026-05-03, and issues #82-#84 (ARM Linux build failure, MIR crash on Chinese text, the wrong-result bug) are unanswered.
Platforms beyond the tested ones if you need AsmJit (arm64 and x86_64 only); x86_64 benchmark results are still marked TBD.

integration.form: shared lib (PostgreSQL extension loaded through jit_provider; one .so/.dylib per backend plus a meta-provider)
integration.dependencies: PostgreSQL 14-18 server headers; sljit (author's patched fork vladich/sljit) and/or AsmJit and/or MIR (patched fork vladich/mir-patched) as sibling source directories; StringZilla headers (required); PCRE2 and yyjson (optional, on by default)
integration.min_toolchain: CMake 3.16, C11 and C++17 compilers (C++20 under MSVC); Release build type by default
integration.platforms: Built and regression-tested on Linux and macOS arm64 (all backends), Linux, FreeBSD and Windows x86_64 (all backends), Linux ppc64le and s390x (sljit only); benchmarks published for Apple M1 Pro only
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable in the usual sense: PostgreSQL backends are single-threaded processes; compiled code is per backend and freed with the query's ResourceOwner, and an experimental 'shared' parallel mode passes code to workers through DSM.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it is a drop-in jit_provider replacement for llvmjit with no SQL changes, but it only pays off with jit_above_cost lowered to about 200-2000, the README recommends keeping jit_inline_above_cost and jit_optimize_above_cost at 500000 (the bench script says lowering them adds about 30 ms), and it is beta quality

gotchas: The published PG18 page was produced by tests/bench_comprehensive.sh (its markdown template matches), not tests/bench_all_backends.sh, which has no llvmjit column. That script runs llvmjit with jit_inline_above_cost and jit_optimize_above_cost at 0 but gives the pg_jitter backends 500000 (comment: they add about 30 ms otherwise), so LLVM is forced into full inlining and -O3 on 20-150 ms queries that default settings would never JIT; most of the llvmjit gap is that compile time (SUM_int execution without it about 45.8 ms vs 42.4 ms sljit, derived from page data).

Each warmup and timed run is a separate `psql -c` call, so every run starts a new backend process: the deform cache (pg_jitter.deform_cache, per-process) cannot carry compiled code between runs, which removes the cache-favouritism worry, but every run also pays per-connection provider loading, which shows up as the 2-2.4 ms penalty on queries where pg_jitter compiled nothing.

Numbers were taken 2026-03-24, before the v0.3.0 tag (2026-03-26); v0.3.1 (2026-03-28) fixed a sparse deform dispatch bug around the same time a sljit segfault was reported (issue #59), and the source now says the 0.3.0-era cap 'incorrectly disabled profitable 1000-column sparse deform', so the Wide1K rows (0.94-0.99x vs interpreter) measured no deform JIT at all.

Several big wins are algorithm swaps inside the JIT (binary-search CASE, PCRE2/StringZilla LIKE and regex) that a different interpreter build could also adopt; upper()/lower() fast paths are disabled in source because collation detection treated en_US.UTF-8 as C and mishandled multibyte text.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The sljit and AsmJit entries cite this same benchmark but are code-generator libraries you would have to build a lowering for; pick pg_jitter when the goal is simply faster JIT inside PostgreSQL (sljit backend for lowest compile time, AsmJit for deform-heavy rows), and look at TPDE or PochiVM-style copy-and-patch only if you are building your own query compiler.
verified_claims_summary: First-party run of pg_jitter 0.3.0 (dated 2026-03-24, two days before the v0.3.0 tag) against PostgreSQL 18.1's interpreter and llvmjit on an Apple M1 Pro (macOS, compiler and flags not stated), median of 3 EXPLAIN ANALYZE execution times per query: compile time mostly 0.04-0.12 ms for sljit (max 0.46 ms), 0.1-0.3 ms for AsmJit (max 2.8 ms) and 0.3-1.3 ms for MIR (16.9 ms on CASE_ts_range_30) vs 17-114 ms (mostly 20-60 ms) for llvmjit forced to full optimization and inlining, and 0.09-2.04 s on the 100-1000-column tables. Against the interpreter, most of the 108 queries land between 0.9x and 1.3x (LIKE_3wild as low as 0.77-0.81x), with 2-7x only on ILIKE/regex, CASE/IN rewrites, LIKE suffix and Interval_arith.
status_note: Apache-2.0 and buildable from source for PG 14-18, but beta quality by its own README, maintained by one author with no commits since 2026-05-03 and an unanswered wrong-result bug (#84), so treat it as an experiment to validate against your own query suite rather than an 'active' production component.
